item.title: Pokémon Pokopia: A Positive Psychology Practice
item.description:
Positive Psychology

Pokémon Pokopia: A Positive Psychology Practice

Personal Perspective: Playing cozy games may develop positive skills for patients.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Happiness needs enjoyment and purpose. Fun tasks tied to helping others promote this.
  • Eliminating failure creates a low-stress space to practice breaking big goals into small and easy steps.
  • FOMO-free gaming builds positive habits and neural pathways translating to real-world change.
Source: Image: The Pokémon Company International

There was a moment during my first playthrough of Pokémon Pokopia that surprised me. I had just completed the rain dance task in Withered Wasteland, and I was working on improving my relationships with the few Pokémon I had lured back into the post-apocalyptic Pokémon world. I looked at the clock and noticed I had been playing for over two hours. I was so absorbed by the game that I hadn't noticed how much time had passed.

Pokémon Pokopia is Nintendo's recent life-simulation game. The premise is that you play as the Pokémon Ditto, who has arrived in an abandoned world and is tasked with restoring the land and coaxing a community of Pokémon back into it.

As a gamer, I've never been drawn to this style of game. The low stakes and repetitive tasks always felt like a grind. However, this title is different, and as a practicing psychiatrist, I see psychological value in this game in particular.

The Concept of Happiness

My favorite framework for how to achieve happiness is outlined by Tal Ben-Shahar in his book Happier: Learn the Secrets to Daily Joy and Lasting Fulfillment. In his book, Ben-Shahar argues that lasting happiness is not achieved by eliminating adversity or by selectively indulging in only pleasurable activities. Happiness comes from the combination of meaning and enjoyment simultaneously.

Pokémon Pokopia is designed to check both those boxes. The gameplay crafting loops are immediately satisfying, and those tasks are in service to something larger. For example, Snorlax needs to build a home, Piplup wants to clean up litter on the beach, and Tangrowth wants social connection. By completing these requests, the player is contributing to a community of Pokémon that they learn to care about.

Flow Without Friction

Pokémon Pokopia does not punish failure. There are no resource scarcities, and the crafting system defaults to basic, easily obtainable resources for almost every item. If you make a mistake, there is always a way to correct it. As the game progresses, it rewards you with abilities that make it even easier to accomplish your tasks.

This gameplay mechanism promotes the psychological concept of "flow," a term coined by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi as a crucial part of positive psychology. When in flow, an individual's attention is absorbed in a particular activity where skill and challenge are closely matched. It depends on three conditions: clear goals, immediate feedback, and a task that pushes ability without exceeding it.

A concrete illustration of this can be seen in the Mysterious Slate puzzle. Scattered across the world are stone slates, each engraved with the form of the Pokémon Unown. The slates must be placed in the correct spot on a mural. When a slate is placed correctly, a chime sounds. As more slates are collected, a picture begins to form of the mythical Pokémon Mew.

The mural puzzle itself consists of a distal goal with underlying subgoals. In the moment, each placement offers a discrete goal with immediate confirmatory feedback. Over weeks of play, the partially completed mural moves towards the distal goal. The nested architecture demonstrates how large tasks can be broken down into incremental steps — something patients with mental health concerns may struggle to do independently.

Daily Rituals

Source: Image: The Pokémon Company International

Positive psychology places a heavy emphasis on daily rituals as a way to enact change. The idea is that change does not occur in one single moment but accumulates through practicing consistent habits over time.

Pokémon Pokopia's design is consistent with this kind of habit formation. I tended to check in at similar times each day to harvest my vegetables, check my empty habitats, and respond to resident requests. Once that was complete, I would step away for a while. Because there are no penalty timers, and real-time events have no stakes, the structure mirrors the daily rituals that are fundamental to building a healthy lifestyle.

Escapism

The space between practicing positive psychology and avoidance is narrow. It is not difficult for video games to cross the line into escapism.

However, escapism is defined by its function. Just as a person can exercise, meditate, play video games in ways that are avoidant, these same activities can be used to mitigate and manage real stressors.

I think Pokémon Pokopia lands on the right side of that line. It is not designed to overpower judgment the way games with variable reward schedules, social pressure, and resource scarcity tend to do. You can play for a discreet amount of time and turn it off. When you pick it up next time, you won't miss out on anything.

The Neurobiology of Change

There is a neurobiological reason why repeated positive experiences in a structured, engaging context lead to lasting pleasure.

Our brains contain neurons that change in response to what we repeatedly do and feel. If you spend 10,000 hours playing basketball, you'll get better at playing basketball. Patterns of thought, attention, and emotional response that get used regularly become more automatic over time. These neural pathways become more efficient and more likely to be activated — strengthening the brain's capacity to access those states more readily.

While the tasks performed in Pokémon Pokopia don't amount to any tangible change in the real world, repeatedly practicing tasks like sticking to a schedule, practicing mindfulness, helping friends, and breaking down goals into individual steps does translate. Practicing them in the game can make it easier to practice them outside.

The Broader Implications

I'll end with another anecdote: I personally found positive change after playing this game.

When I finished cleaning up all the trash on Bleak Beach, I thought to myself, Why not apply this to my own life? I went to my basement, cleaned up all the junk I'd left lying around over the years, and I felt good about it. I would imagine I'm not the only person inspired to make small but positive changes after playing the game.

item.title: Why Do Controlling Parents Praise More?
item.description:
Parenting

Why Do Controlling Parents Praise More?

By every external measure, my life looked like a success story.

Posted July 27, 2026

I ranked 56th out of one million students on Türkiye's university entrance exam, earned a master's degree from Harvard as a Fulbright and TEV scholar, and completed my Ph.D. at Cambridge, with a year as a visiting PhD student at MIT. Then, with my final degree in hand, I was blindsided by an anxiety I could not explain.

It took me years to understand why. My happiness rested entirely on academic achievement because somewhere along the way, I had come to believe my family would love me only if I were successful at school. In school, the rules were clear: study hard, get the grade, earn approval. Professional life offered no such clarity. Even when I met my own standards, I couldn't be sure others agreed. What if I couldn't maintain my success? Would my family still love me? Would anyone?

I was in a trap.

I can trace how that belief formed. My family motivated me the way many loving parents do: with rewards and praise and, when those fell short, with subtle criticism. Each carried the same underlying message: "You are loved when you meet my expectations."

Years later, as a researcher, I kept returning to a question that was both scientific and personal: What if praise and rewards sometimes reveal something deeper than encouragement?

When Praise Becomes Controlling

A classic study by Richard Ryan and his colleagues (Ryan, Mims, and Koestner, 1983), co-founders of self-determination theory with the late Edward Deci (Ryan and Deci, 2000), asked university students to solve puzzles with hidden figures while receiving different kinds of praise.

One group received informational praise: "You did very well on that one." Another group received controlling praise: "You did very well on that one, just as you should."

That small phrase, "just as you should," added pressure and expectation.

Later, when students were left alone with the puzzles, those who had received controlling praise spent less time working on them voluntarily. The lesson is powerful: Praise can become controlling when it quietly communicates, "You are meeting my standard."

This is where our research began. Rather than asking whether praise is good or bad, we asked a different question:

What kind of parents most often rely on praise and rewards?

Praise and Criticism Travel Together

To answer this, I first developed and validated a new scale measuring how parents use rewards (Bolat, 2023). More than 700 parents participated. Two distinct patterns emerged.

Some parents used rewards mainly as encouragement. They agreed with statements such as “I motivate my child with rewards.” Or, “I use rewards to encourage good behavior.” Others used rewards to gain compliance. They agreed with statements such as “I use rewards to make my child do what I want.” Or, “I promise rewards to get my child to do things they don’t want to do.”

We also measured how often parents praised and criticized their children. We also assessed parental disrespect using Brian Barber's well-established psychological control disrespect scale, which includes harsh criticism, public embarrassment, ridicule, and comparisons with other children (Barber and colleagues, 2012).

One might expect parents who frequently praise and reward their children to criticize and disrespect them less.

We found the opposite.

Parents who used rewards more often also reported more criticism and psychological disrespect. The same pattern appeared for praise. Strikingly, this was true even when parents said they used rewards to encourage rather than control.

That raised a deeper question:

Why would praise go hand in hand with criticism and disrespect?

To answer this question, we conducted another study (Bolat and Kara, 2023).

Two Sides of the Same Coin

We examined parents' use of rewards, praise, punishment threats, and autonomy support (acknowledging children's feelings and perspectives).

Three distinct parenting profiles emerged.

The first group (high controllers) relied heavily on rewards and praise. They were also more likely to threaten punishment, criticize, and pressure their children. They were less likely to acknowledge their children's feelings.

The second group (low controllers) used fewer rewards and less punishment but still showed moderate levels of control.

The third group (autonomy supporters) looked very different.

These parents used rewards and praise the least. They rarely threatened punishment. They showed the highest respect for their children's autonomy and were most likely to empathize with their children.

The Connection between Praise and Criticism

Our findings may help explain the connection between praise and criticism. Rewards and punishments, like praise and criticism, often appear to be opposites. But psychologically, they may come from the same source: the desire to control another person's behavior. Both rely on consequences rather than understanding.

Of course, this does not mean every parent who praises or rewards their child is controlling.

How These Parenting Styles Look in Everyday Life

Imagine a child who refuses to practice the piano.

One parent says, "If you practice for twenty minutes, we'll go out for ice cream." Another says, "If you don't practice, there won't be any screen time tonight."

The emotional tone is different, but both parents are asking the same question:

"How can I get my child to do what I want?"

Now imagine a third parent who asks:

"You usually enjoy playing. What might be getting in the way, and how can I help?"

When children feel understood instead of managed, respected instead of controlled, approval seeking declines, and motivation is more likely to come from within.

When Praise Becomes a Disguise for Control

Looking back, I do not think praise was the problem. Control was. Praise became one of its most socially acceptable disguises. My parents loved me deeply, but too often the message I heard was, “You are loved when you meet my expectations.”

Children who feel loved for who they are can enjoy success without depending on it.

I know because I spent decades chasing approval before I realized what I had been searching for was not achievement. It was unconditional acceptance, and praise may not provide it.

item.title: The “I’m Bored” Trap Isn’t About Your Kid’s Brain
item.description:
Parenting

The “I’m Bored” Trap Isn’t About Your Kid’s Brain

What if your kid's boredom is about your own parenting anxiety?

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Our urge to fix boredom may be driven by our own anxiety.
  • Adults struggle with downtime just as much.
  • True regulation starts with us regulating ourselves as parents.

We’ve all been here. You’re standing in the kitchen, dinner is half-cooked, and your child wanders in, drops his arms like lead weights, and lets out those two dreaded words: “I’m bored.”

We all know that we should encourage our children to come up with ideas about what they could do instead of reaching for an iPad, phone, computer, or video game. But, let’s be real – saying something like, “What do you think you can do?” or “I’m sure you’ll come up with a great idea,” means that you’re going to have a child or teen or even a young adult who is going to look at you and repeat, “I’m bored.”

When our kids say those two dreaded words, “I’m bored,” a tiny, panic-driven alarm goes off in your brain. As a parent, you may feel the urge to fix that boredom and to offer a project or set up a play date or take them somewhere “fun.” Most of the time, our ideas are shot down with a dramatic groan or grumble. We all want to grow creative, self-sufficient kids, but we also feel the need to scramble and “fix” our child's boredom. What if that boredom is not about their development at all, but is rather about our own low tolerance for their temporary distress or boredom??

Is this about our own discomfort?

Here is the uncomfortable truth: We are asking our children to master a skill that we, as adults, may not have figured out ourselves.

Consider this famous 2014 study published in Science: Researchers placed participants in a room alone for 15 minutes with nothing to do. They were given a choice: sit quietly with their thoughts or press a button to give themselves a mild electric shock. The result? A significant portion of participants chose to shock themselves rather than sit in silence with their own minds.

Ask yourself this question: When was the last time you stood in a grocery store line for two minutes without pulling out your phone? When was the last time you sat at a red light, rode an elevator, or waited for a doctor’s appointment without scrolling through social media or checking your email? Most of us can’t survive thirty seconds of unstructured downtime without seeking some sort of entertainment or information seeking.

So it should be no surprise to us when our child or teenager struggles to sit in the back of the car for twenty minutes without a screen. It’s not a failure of imagination for our children; we don’t access our own silence or thoughts with ease either.

Why do we panic when we hear the words, "I'm Bored?”

When a child whines about being bored, it hits a cluster of deeply ingrained parental triggers, such as our worry about not being a “good parent” by filling our child’s every moment with enrichment, activity, learning, and bonding. We also may be trying to avoid conflict by keeping our kids occupied and “happy.” Bored kids are not happy or quiet kids. Bored kids tend to whine, pick fights with siblings, or create chaos. Perhaps we feel that by fixing the boredom we’re preventing the chaos that comes with bored children. Another reason could be that seeing our kids squirm in their unstructured time reflects our own deep discomfort with slowing down. Their agitation may be shining light on our own restlessness. When we rush to fix their boredom, we aren't just rescuing them from discomfort. Perhaps we are also rescuing ourselves from the discomfort of watching them struggle.

Regulate yourself first

If we want our kids to build emotional resilience and learn how to navigate unstructured time, the work doesn't start with teaching them how to play quietly or find creative ways to keep them occupied without screens. Rather, it starts with training ourselves to tolerate their boredom and the “noise” they make when they are feeling bored.

The next time your child hits you with "I'm bored," try shifting your focus inward. That is, pause and take note of your own discomfort. Notice the tightening in your chest or the urge to hand them a device or come up with some great idea just to keep the peace. Acknowledge that their boredom is not an emergency, nor is it a sign that you are failing as a parent.

Try to validate without fixing your child or teen's boredom. Instead of offering ideas or quickly planning an activity, keep it simple and grounded. Say something like, "I wonder what you can find as something fun to do. I know you’re bored, but it’s also okay to be bored.” Set that boundary, step back, and wait. Let them know that finding an activity is their job, not yours. Then, let them sit with that discomfort as you sit with yours. Let them groan, wander around the room, or sit on the floor looking miserable.

Boredom isn't a deficiency you need to cure. Instead, it’s more of that struggle of having to transition from finishing something and finding something else without a parent stepping in to tell them what that next thing is. It’s turning inward to problem-solve or come up with something without adult intervention.

If you can stay calm through this process, without rushing in to “fix it,” you give your child the ultimate gift: space to figure out who they are when no one is orchestrating the show. This will also help you to manage your own discomfort, especially as you watch your children “figure it out.”
